title: How Much Do Metal Studs Cost in Canada? Guide
description: Learn how much metal studs cost in Canada, what changes the price, how to estimate quantities, and how to compare supplier quotes.
html:
There is no single Canada-wide price for metal studs. Your material quote changes with stud depth, gauge, length, spacing, framing role, quantity, track, accessories, delivery, and taxes. Budget the complete package instead of multiplying one retail price by wall length.

This guide explains how to build a preliminary budget, separate material-only costs from installed framing, and prepare a comparable Canadian supplier request. The examples are hypothetical estimating exercises, not market quotes.

The short answer: metal studs do not have one Canadian price

Metal studs are priced by product specification and order conditions, not by a universal national rate. A short, light-gauge interior partition and a tall, load-bearing exterior wall may both be called metal stud framing, but they require different products and should not share the same budget assumption.

  • Studs only: vertical members, usually priced by piece, bundle, or quoted quantity.
  • Framing materials: studs plus track, fasteners, clips, channels, bridging, and other components.
  • Installed framing: materials plus layout, cutting, handling, fastening, and labor.
  • Complete wall assembly: installed framing plus insulation, gypsum board, finishing, services coordination, equipment, and other specified work.

A project-based quote is the reliable next step because configuration, quantity, delivery location, and project requirements materially affect the result.

What a metal stud framing budget actually includes

Metal stud framing uses vertical studs with horizontal track at the floor, ceiling, or other perimeter conditions. The assembly may also need standard or deflection track, clips, bridging channel, furring channel, resilient channel, fasteners, trim, or custom profiles.

A studs-only calculation can understate the budget. Include extra members at corners, intersections, jambs, openings, headers, and backing, then price track, fasteners, connectors, channels, waste, packaging, handling, freight, and applicable taxes.

Insulation, drywall, joint treatment, paint, electrical and mechanical work, and labor are separate cost lines unless the quotation expressly includes them. Ask every bidder to state inclusions and exclusions.

Classify the framing before comparing prices

First decide whether the wall is non-load-bearing or structural. Non-load-bearing partitions generally fall into the light-gauge category. Load-bearing, exterior, tall-wall, floor, ceiling, shaft-wall, and wind-related work may require heavier or engineered framing.

  • If the wall supports only its finishes: investigate non-load-bearing light-gauge framing and coordinate stud, track, spacing, height, and deflection requirements.
  • If it supports floors, roofs, cladding, or other structural loads: price the designed member, connections, track, and engineering information.
  • If it is exterior, unusually tall, or part of a floor or roof system: do not use an interior drywall-stud allowance as the budget basis.
  • If it includes movement, seismic, fire, acoustic, shaft, or unusual geometry requirements: include the relevant track, clips, channels, documents, and coordination.

The category is only a starting point. Drawings, design criteria, and technical review still control the selection.

The project inputs that change a Canadian metal stud quote

Two quotes can differ substantially even when both list steel studs. Give suppliers the same information so you compare equivalent materials and scope.

Dimensions, gauge, and quantity

Stud depth, flange configuration, length, spacing, wall height, wall length, wall type, gauge, and total quantity affect the material requirement. A long member may cost more per piece than a shorter one, while a large order may be priced differently from a small pickup quantity.

Openings and layout complexity

Doors, windows, access panels, corners, intersections, soffits, offsets, and returns add members and cutting. A straight-wall calculation is only a starting point.

Track and accessories

Track must match the stud and wall condition. Slotted or deflection track, deep track, bridging channel, clips, resilient channel, furring channel, and finishing sections each add material and coordination requirements.

Delivery and commercial terms

Delivery location, pickup or freight, order size, site access, unloading conditions, timing, packaging, and taxes affect the amount you actually pay. Long, lightweight members can require considerable delivery space, so request freight as a separate line.

Standard versus custom material

Standard profiles are easier to compare than custom roll-formed profiles. A custom request may require drawings, engineering input, production setup, special quantities, or additional documentation.

Common stud sizes and gauges: what they mean for the budget

Canadian suppliers commonly use several member depths for interior and structural framing. A size list helps prepare a request, but it cannot select the correct stud without the wall function, height, spacing, loads, and assembly requirements.

Member depthPossible planning contextConfirm before pricing
1-5/8 inchesShallow partitions or limited-depth furring.Finish thickness, service space, height, spacing, and gauge.
2 inchesCompact interior framing where a narrow cavity is suitable.Profile, availability, board and insulation needs, load role, and track.
2-1/2 inchesInterior partitions needing a modest service cavity.Length, gauge, spacing, height, deflection, and openings.
3-5/8 inchesPartitions requiring more cavity depth for services or insulation.Assembly, acoustic or fire requirements, gauge, spacing, and track.
6 inchesDeeper interior or exterior-related framing conditions.Structural role, exposure, height, bracing, connections, and documents.

Yes, 2-inch metal studs are made in general Canadian practice. That does not mean every supplier stocks every length, gauge, or profile, or that a 2-inch member suits your wall. Request the exact depth, flange, return, gauge, length, spacing, and application.

Gauge comparisons also need context. A 25-gauge interior member should not be compared with a heavier structural stud as though they were interchangeable alternatives.

A repeatable method for estimating studs, track, and waste

For a straight wall, use:

Basic studs = ceiling function (wall length ÷ spacing) + 1

For example, a 40-foot wall at 16 inches on center is 480 inches long. The basic count is ceiling function (480 ÷ 16) + 1, or 31 studs, before corners, openings, end conditions, and waste.

Add members for corners, intersections, partition ends, door and window jambs, headers, sills, backing, and doubled conditions. For a simple partition with one floor and one ceiling track:

Basic track = wall length × 2

Add track for returns, offsets, bulkheads, openings, separate wall segments, or alternate head-of-wall details. Apply a clearly stated waste allowance after layout additions are included. Waste depends on cuts, geometry, member length, openings, damage, and takeoff control.

Worked example: turn a hypothetical wall into a material budget

Consider a hypothetical 40-foot-long by 10-foot-high interior partition with 16-inch stud spacing, one door opening, 12-foot stud lengths, one floor track, one ceiling track, and a provisional 10 percent waste allowance.

  1. Convert 40 feet to 480 inches.
  2. Calculate the field count: ceiling function (480 ÷ 16) + 1 = 31 studs.
  3. Add door jambs, header, end conditions, intersections, and backing shown on the drawings. Call this addition O.
  4. Calculate basic track: 40 feet × 2 = 80 linear feet.
  5. Add track for returns, openings, or alternate head-of-wall conditions. Call this addition T.
  6. Apply the waste allowance to the quantities after layout additions.
  • Studs: (31 + O) × 1.10, rounded up to whole members.
  • Track: (80 linear feet + T) × 1.10, rounded according to the supplier’s sale unit and requested lengths.
  • Accessories: quantities from door, corner, intersection, deflection, bridging, and finish details.
  • Freight and taxes: added as separate quote lines.

Preliminary material total = stud amount + track amount + accessory amount + packaging + freight + taxes

Do not present a retail listing from another region as a Canada-wide average. Use the exercise to identify quantities and missing scope, then obtain a project-specific quote. The same method scales to larger commercial work by separating wall types, heights, spacing, openings, and delivery phases.

Material-only versus installed framing cost

A stud-material budget cannot be converted into a universal installed price. Labor depends on layout complexity, wall height, access, handling, cutting, openings, substrate conditions, crew productivity, schedule, equipment, and regional labor conditions.

Define the quote boundary. “Framing installed” may include layout, studs, track, clips, bridging, and fastening, but exclude insulation, drywall, finishing, painting, demolition, waste removal, lifts, or service coordination. Another contractor may include some of these items.

For a fair comparison, ask each contractor to identify materials, quantities, labor, equipment, openings, corners, special details, insulation, drywall, finishing, freight, taxes, allowances, exclusions, and change-order assumptions.

How to request and compare Canadian supplier quotes

For a commercial project, compare technical fit, documentation, quantity capability, delivery scope, communication, and quote completeness, not merely the lowest unexplained stud price.

  • Project: site location, access, pickup or freight preference, and required delivery window.
  • Application: non-load-bearing interior, load-bearing, exterior, ceiling, shaft-wall, furring, or another defined use.
  • Geometry: wall lengths, heights, openings, corners, intersections, returns, and wall types.
  • Member specification: depth, gauge or design requirement, flange and return, length, spacing, and finish.
  • Related components: track, clips, bridging channel, furring or resilient channel, fasteners, trims, and backing.
  • Quantity: takeoff quantity, waste allowance, bundle or piece requirements, and phased delivery.
  • Documents: drawings, schedules, load information, specifications, technical data, submittals, and safety documents.
  • Commercial terms: material prices, freight, packaging, taxes, validity period, exclusions, and assumptions.

For a Vaughan or Ontario project, provide the supplier with the application, quantities, specifications, delivery location, and required documents so the quote can be priced against a defined scope. Confirm the exact product, quantity, availability, and delivery terms for the individual order.

Questions that deserve a project-specific answer

Are metal studs priced per piece or by another unit?

They may be quoted by piece, bundle, linear measure, or another supplier-defined sale unit. Compare total quantity, length, gauge, and freight rather than a unit number without its sale basis.

Do 2-inch metal studs cost less than 3-5/8-inch studs?

Not necessarily. Depth, gauge, length, profile, quantity, freight, and availability all affect the quote. The two depths may also serve different wall requirements.

Why can delivery change the cost so much?

Long framing members require space, handling, and unloading arrangements. Distance, shipment size, site access, delivery timing, and pickup versus delivery can materially change the delivered total.

How should I compare light-gauge and heavy-gauge quotes?

Confirm that both suppliers priced the same framing role and design requirement. Then compare depth, gauge, length, spacing, track, connections, accessories, documents, freight, taxes, and exclusions.

From a preliminary budget to a reviewable order

A defensible metal stud budget has three parts: clear framing classification, measured quantities, and a quote that states the complete material and delivery scope. Once aligned, you can compare suppliers without confusing an individual stud price with a finished framing package.

If your project uses non-load-bearing interior partitions, review non-load-bearing light-gauge steel studs from Dass Metal Products, then confirm the exact product, quantity, availability, and delivery terms for your order.
